chapter: Return to Chicago: the Blue Note and Rupneck's
title: An all-white band at Rupneck's and Chicago's segregated locals
summary: Hodes ended up with an all-white band at Rupneck's. DeMichael relays Red Saunders's account of the understanding about black bands in the Loop.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: one man. So it didn't work out. Two weeks, I found out I couldn't do a single, there wasn't a jazz joint special. So I came back to Chicago and Skeak came up with a Rupneck's job, and here I am, involved in a jazz band. And again, it turned out to be all white, either Skeak's doing or -- I don't know. Chicago was not against me having a mixed band at the Blue Note. But, again, they told me, in Chicago you ask questions and go halfway.
And I know that Lee Collins, they were jamming with Lee Collins here and there. But there was still strictly white bands and black bands.

Yeah. Red Saunders, who was very close to the black union, said there was an understanding that black musicians could only work certain places in the Loop. Petillo's union - not that, but they didn't want mixed bands and they didn't want black musicians, black bands, playing too much in the Loop. And he and Harry Gray, the president of the black local, came to this disagreement.

And that of course killed my act at that time. And of course, that puts you at the mercy of the talent available. And usually, the talent available, there may be something wrong with it if it's very good. It's either they get too loaded or something, or they show up late. Because if they are very good, they're probably out of your reach, or they can go and get their own job. And this you find out.
